Original heading

Concerning Leviathan.

God illustrates his power through Leviathan

The Lord continued showing Job his own weakness and God's unlimited power through a description of Leviathan.

Henry reports that readers debated whether the creature was a whale or a crocodile.

He does not settle the question.

God demonstrated that Job was unable to subdue this mighty animal, then displayed something of the divine power that had made it.

If the language used about Leviathan shows such frightening strength, what language could fully express the power of God's wrath?

Let us recognize our own sinfulness and weakness and honor the majesty of God.

Let us take up the place and responsibilities he has assigned to us, cease depending proudly on our own wisdom, and give every part of the glory to our gracious God and Savior.

Every good gift comes from him and has been entrusted to us for a purpose.

Remembering both the Giver and his purpose, may we walk humbly with the Lord.
classic_reading:
[Job.41.1]
Chapter 41
Concerning Leviathan.
--The description of the Leviathan, is yet further to convince Job of his own weakness, and of God's almighty power. Whether this Leviathan be a whale or a crocodile, is disputed. The Lord, having showed Job how unable he was to deal with the Leviathan, sets forth his own power in that mighty creature. If such language describes the terrible force of Leviathan, what words can express the power of God's wrath? Under a humbling sense of our own vileness, let us revere the Divine Majesty; take and fill our allotted place, cease from our own wisdom, and give all glory to our gracious God and Saviour. Remembering from whom every good gift cometh, and for what end it was given, let us walk humbly with the Lord.

Job submits humbly to God (verses 1–6)

Job now recognized his guilt.

He stopped making excuses and abhorred himself as a sinner in heart and conduct, especially for his complaints against God.

He was ashamed and repented.

When the Spirit of grace enlightens our understanding, the new knowledge we gain of God's character is as much greater than what we previously knew as seeing something for ourselves is greater than hearing reports about it.

God reveals his Son to us through other people's teaching.

But through the Spirit he reveals his Son within us (Galatians 1:16), changing us into his likeness (2 Corinthians 3:18).

When we recognize our sins, we must humble ourselves deeply for them.

Henry says self-abhorrence accompanies true repentance.

God will bring those he loves to worship him humbly.

Saving grace moves us to confess sin without trying to justify ourselves.

Job prays for his friends (verses 7–9)

After Job was convinced of his faults and humbled in repentance, the Lord recognized him, comforted him and honored him.

Satan had tried to prove Job a hypocrite.

His three friends had condemned him as a wicked man.

But when God approves a servant, the accusations of others matter little.

The friends had misrepresented God.

They had made earthly prosperity a sign of the true church and suffering certain evidence of God's anger.

Job had recognized more clearly that judgment and reward belong chiefly to the coming world.

In that respect he had spoken more rightly about God than they had.

Job prayed and offered sacrifice on behalf of the very friends who had hurt him.

In this he was like Christ, who prayed for his persecutors and always lives to intercede for sinners.

Henry regards Job's friends as good men who genuinely belonged to God, despite their errors.

The Lord would not let them continue in their mistakes any more than he had allowed Job to continue in his.

He had humbled Job by speaking from the whirlwind.

He humbled the friends in another way.

They were no longer to argue.

They had to unite through a sacrifice and a prayer, so that reconciliation could be achieved.

Believers may differ over lesser matters of judgment, yet they belong together in Christ, the great Sacrifice.

Therefore they should love one another and bear with one another.

When God was displeased with Job's friends, he still showed them the way to peace.

The offense begins on our side, but reconciliation begins through God's mercy.

Peace with him comes only in his appointed way and on his terms.

Those who understand how precious that peace is will accept even humbling conditions with gratitude.

Job did not use his vindication to insult his friends.

Once God had received him graciously, he readily forgave them.

In all our prayers and service, we should seek God's approval, not people's admiration.

Job's prosperity is restored (<reference osisRef="Job.42.10-Job.42.17" resp="BibleResourcesOriginalSourceRangeInModernSectionHeading">verses 10–17</reference>)

At the beginning of the book, Job's patience during suffering provided an example.

The conclusion gives encouragement to follow that example by showing his joyful end.

His trials began through Satan's hostility, which God restrained.

His restoration began through God's mercy, which Satan could not oppose.

Notice the turning point.

Job's possessions were not restored while he continued arguing with his friends.

Restoration came when he prayed for them.

The Lord is pleased by warm devotion, not heated disputes.

He doubled Job's possessions.

We may lose much for the Lord, but we will never ultimately lose anything because of the Lord.

Whether he grants health or material advantages in this life or not, those who endure suffering patiently according to his will will be happy in the end.

Job's wealth increased.

The Lord's blessing gives people the ability to gain wealth and grants success to honest work.

Sometimes the last days of a godly life become its best days, the latest acts its best service and the final comforts its sweetest.

The believer's path resembles the light of morning, growing brighter and brighter until the perfect day.

[Job.42.1-Job.42.6]
Chapter 42
Chapter Outline
Job humbly submits unto God. | (1-6) |
Job intercedes for his friends. | (7-9) |
His renewed prosperity. | (10-17) |
Verses 1-6
Job was now sensible of his guilt; he would no longer speak in his own excuse; he abhorred himself as a sinner in heart and life, especially for murmuring against God, and took shame to himself. When the understanding is enlightened by the Spirit of grace, our knowledge of Divine things as far exceeds what we had before, as the sight of the eyes excels report and common fame. By the teachings of men, God reveals his Son to us; but by the teachings of his Spirit he reveals his Son in us, [Gal.1.16] Ga 1:16, and changes us into the same image, [2Cor.3.18] 2Co 3:18. It concerns us to be deeply humbled for the sins of which we are convinced. Self-loathing is ever the companion of true repentance. The Lord will bring those whom he loveth, to adore him in self-abasement; while true grace will always lead them to confess their sins without self-justifying.
[Job.42.7-Job.42.9]
Verses 7-9
After the Lord had convinced and humbled Job, and brought him to repentance, he owned him, comforted him, and put honour upon him. The devil had undertaken to prove Job a hypocrite, and his three friends had condemned him as a wicked man; but if God say, Well done, thou good and faithful servant, it is of little consequence who says otherwise. Job's friends had wronged God, by making prosperity a mark of the true church, and affliction a certain proof of God's wrath. Job had referred things to the future judgment and the future state, more than his friends, therefore he spake of God that which was right, better than his friends had done. And as Job prayed and offered sacrifice for those that had grieved and wounded his spirit, so Christ prayed for his persecutors, and ever lives, making intercession for the transgressors. Job's friends were good men, and belonged to God, and He would not let them be in their mistake any more than Job; but having humbled him by a discourse out of the whirlwind, he takes another way to humble them. They are not to argue the matter again, but they must agree in a sacrifice and a prayer, and that must reconcile them, Those who differ in judgment about lesser things, yet are one in Christ the great Sacrifice, and ought therefore to love and bear with one another. When God was angry with Job's friends, he put them in a way to make peace with him. Our quarrels with God always begin on our part, but the making peace begins on his. Peace with God is to be had only in his own way, and upon his own terms. These will never seem hard to those who know how to value this blessing: they will be glad of it, like Job's friends, upon any terms, though ever so humbling. Job did not insult over his friends, but God being graciously reconciled to him, he was easily reconciled to them. In all our prayers and services we should aim to be accepted of the Lord; not to have praise of men, but to please God. ( [Job.42.10-Job.42.17] Job 42:10-17)
[Job.42.10-Job.42.17]
Verses 10-17
In the beginning of this book we had Job's patience under his troubles, for an example; here, for our encouragement to follow that example, we have his happy end. His troubles began in Satan's malice, which God restrained; his restoration began in God's mercy, which Satan could not oppose. Mercy did not return when Job was disputing with his friends, but when he was praying for them. God is served and pleased with our warm devotions, not with our warm disputes. God doubled Job's possessions. We may lose much for the Lord, but we shall not lose any thing by him. Whether the Lord gives us health and temporal blessings or not, if we patiently suffer according to his will, in the end we shall be happy. Job's estate increased. The blessing of the Lord makes rich; it is he that gives us power to get wealth, and gives success in honest endeavours. The last days of a good man sometimes prove his best, his last works his best works, his last comforts his best comforts; for his path, like that of the morning light, shines more and more unto the perfect day.
